prompt.context: Your client is a successful entrepreneur based in Manhattan. She is always thinking of creative ways to start new businesses. Her latest idea is to build a floating hotel — think of a skyscraper on a barge, and the combined structure is seaworthy. Today is October 1, and she must make a decision ASAP. Her preferred construction company and barge manufacturer have openings on November 1 for projects. If she misses this window it will be another two years before both companies can simultaneously work together. The entrepreneur hires you to assess whether she should spend $20M to build a seaworthy floating hotel.
prompt.question: Should the client spend $20M to build a seaworthy floating hotel? Her financial objective is a 20% ROI in the first year.

clarifying_info.q: Can the hotel actually travel on water?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, the hotel can travel on water like a sea vessel.

clarifying_info.q: How long does construction and validation take?
Where will the hotel and barge be fabricated?

clarifying_info.a: $20M is a sunk investment representing all labour, material, and testing costs to manufacture and validate the seaworthy floating hotel.
20% ROI in the first year of operation.

clarifying_info.q: When does the client want to begin operating?
clarifying_info.a: She wants to begin operating as soon as construction and testing conclude — that is, November 1 of the following year.

clarifying_info.q: Does the client have sufficient funds?
clarifying_info.a: Assume the client has sufficient funds.

framework: Market Analysis: size and growth of travel & tourism industry, competitive landscape (direct and substitute competitors), regulatory environment
Location Strategy: identify two locations that exploit seasonality to maximise revenues year-round using the hotel's ability to travel via the Atlantic Ocean
Financial Analysis — Revenue: calculate annual room revenue and first-floor revenue for each city/season
Financial Analysis — Cost: identify variable cost (VC) and fixed cost (FC) buckets; calculate total annual costs for Manhattan and Miami
Financial Analysis — ROI: compute profit = total revenue minus total costs; compute ROI = profit / investment; compare against 20% target

questions.prompt: Part 1 — Market Analysis: What does the competitive landscape look like for a seaworthy floating hotel on the US East Coast?
questions.guidance: Candidate should note: (1) No other seaworthy floating hotels exist in the US (east or west coast) — first-mover advantage. (2) Indirect competitors are numerous and fragmented: chain hotels and motels, small business operators, bed & breakfasts, campers/RVs, weekly apartment rentals, etc. (3) The travel & tourism industry shows good growth in tourist cities. (4) Government regulations will be addressed and met during the construction and validation phases. (5) The exact market size and share are unknown. Candidate should also note client is only considering the US East Coast market.

questions.prompt: Part 2 — Location Strategy: What two locations should the client consider, and when should the hotel be docked at each?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify that the hotel can travel between two locations per year (two trips per year, two locations). The key insight is to exploit seasonality: high season in Manhattan is May 1 – October 31 (late spring, summer, early fall); high season in Miami is November 1 – April 30 (late fall, winter, early spring). Ideal answer: dock in Miami from November 1 to April 30, and in Manhattan from May 1 to October 31. Both periods are high season, maximising revenues year-round. The hotel operates while docked; transit (2.5 days each way) means the hotel operates 360 days per year (365 minus 5 transit days).

math.setup: 365 days per year minus 2 trips x 2.5 transit days each = 360 operating days
steps: 2 trips x 2.5 days per trip = 5 transit days
180 days in Miami (high season), 180 days in Manhattan (high season)
math.answer: 360 operating days per year; 180 days per city

questions.prompt: Part 3A — Revenue Calculation: Calculate total annual revenue for the seaworthy floating hotel.
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognise that both cities are in high season simultaneously (the hotel travels between them), so only high-season rates apply. Low-season numbers provided are a distraction. Revenue is identical in Miami and Manhattan so calculation can be doubled. Hotel structure: 26 floors total, floors 2-26 have rooms (25 floors), 5x5 grid = 25 rooms per floor = 625 rooms total. High-season room rate: $200/room/day; occupancy: 80%. First-floor revenue (restaurant/bar/shop): $200,000/month in high season. Each city season = 180 days = 6 months.

math.setup: Room revenue per city = rooms x occupancy x rate x days; First-floor revenue per city = $200,000/month x 6 months; Total annual revenue = 2 x (room revenue + first-floor revenue)
steps: Total rooms = 25 floors x 25 rooms = 625 rooms
Room revenue per city = 625 x 80% x $200 x 180 = 625 x 0.8 x 200 x 180
First-floor revenue per city = $200,000 x 6 months = $1,200,000 per city

Note: casebook states total annual revenue = $38,400,000; discrepancy may reflect rounding or slightly different occupancy/rate assumptions in the casebook's own exhibit. Use $38,400,000 per the official answer key.
math.answer: $38,400,000 total annual revenue (per casebook answer key)

questions.prompt: Part 3B — Cost Analysis: What cost buckets should the client consider, and what are the total annual costs?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify variable costs (VC) and fixed costs (FC). Key VC: housekeeping (internal and external — federal regulations mandate daily exterior inspections regardless of occupancy), food & drink, etc. Key FC: docking fees (significant), insurance (massive), yearly regulatory fees, etc. Important note: VC and FC are the same in high and low seasons (seasonality does not affect costs). VC applies to all 625 rooms every day (100% occupancy assumption for costs, not revenue occupancy). Cost data: Manhattan VC = $150/room/day; Manhattan FC = $3M/season. Miami VC = $100/room/day; Miami FC = $1M/season. Each season = 180 days.

math.setup: Total cost per city = (rooms x VC per room per day x days) + FC per season; Total annual cost = Manhattan total + Miami total
steps: Manhattan VC = 25 floors x 25 rooms x $150/day x 180 days = 625 x $150 x 180 = $16,875,000

questions.prompt: Part 3C — ROI: Does the hotel meet the client's financial objective of 20% ROI in the first year?
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute profit as total revenue minus total costs, then ROI as profit divided by investment. The ROI of ~31.4% exceeds the 20% target, so the project meets the financial objective.

math.setup: Profit = Total Revenue - Total Costs; ROI = Profit / Investment x 100%

brainstorming.prompt: What risks should the client consider, and how can they be mitigated?

categories.name: Occupancy Risk
ideas: Risk of being first seaworthy floating hotel and not achieving the anticipated 80% occupancy rate
Mitigation: run promotions and advance sales to secure early bookings; since ROI exceeds objective, the client can trim the top line and still meet the financial target

categories.name: Competitive Entry
ideas: Competitors will enter the market due to strong profits, potentially reducing occupancy and increasing docking fees
Mitigation: as first mover with at least a one-year lead, secure multi-year contracts for docking fees in Miami and Manhattan

categories.name: Regulatory Risk
ideas: New or changing maritime and hospitality regulations could raise costs or delay operations
Mitigation: engage regulators early; build compliance into construction and validation phases

categories.name: Operational Risk
ideas: Weather or mechanical issues could delay transit between cities, reducing operating days
Mitigation: build buffer into schedule; carry appropriate marine insurance

recommendation: The client should proceed with construction on November 1 to fabricate the seaworthy floating hotel
The hotel achieves a projected ROI of approximately 31%, well above the 20% target
The hotel's unique ability to operate as a sea vessel enables it to capitalise on high tourism seasons in both Miami (November–April) and Manhattan (May–October)
The client also has adequate funding to finance the project
risks: Occupancy may fall short of the projected 80% as the first-ever seaworthy floating hotel, compressing revenue
Competitor entry could erode market position and drive up docking fees at key ports
Maritime and hospitality regulatory changes could increase costs or restrict operations
next_steps: Ensure contracts are drawn up with the hotel and barge manufacturers to secure the November 1 construction slot
Scout and secure port/docking locations in Manhattan and Miami, ideally with multi-year agreements to lock in docking fees
Begin an advertising campaign at least 6 months in advance of the hotel's opening (i.e., by May 1 of the following year)
